newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS-ANZ fees offset margin squeeze.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-ANZ fees offset margin squeeze.

text.p: The Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd (ANZ) forecast on Wednesday that lending growth and higher fee income would continue to offset the effect of falling interest margins.
The bank said it had performed as expected in the first quarter of the year to September 30, 1997.

ANZ said also that core costs were stable at the level reached in the second half of 1996 and that the bank had agreed with the Finance Sector Union (FSU) to cut staff by attrition rather than forced layoffs.

"ANZ's financial performance in the first quarter of the current year has been very much as we expected. The anticipated fall in interest margins in Australia is occurring, flowing particularly from the reductions in mortgage lending rates in the latter part of 1996," ANZ Chairman Charles Goode told the group's annual meeting.
"However, this is being offset by continued growth in lending assets and increased fee income," Goode said.
He said the bank's core costs, which excluded retrenchment costs and direct revenue costs, were stable at the level of the second half of 1996.
"We see no sign of deterioration in our asset quality, which remains very good," he added.
Australian business conditions would continue to be subdued for the next six months, with the prospect of an acceleration in economic activity later in 1997.
Goode said ANZ expected to see tangible evidence of the benefits of the restructuring of its domestic banking businesses in Australia and New Zealand.
Staff reductions would be necessary due to the changing face of banking, which was moving away from traditional branch networks towards electronic delivered services.
But the bank had yet to agree with the FSU on exactly how it would reduce staff numbers, although the two agreed attrition was better than sackings.

"Some of the areas we would agree with are that what change or lost staff are necessary or eventuate from the restructuring, should be by attrition," Goode said in response to a question from ANZ shareholder, Tony Beck, who is also joint national secretary of the FSU.
"We are also putting more emphasis on retraining," he said.
Goode said that profit growth should come from the ANZ's international operations.

"There is significant potential growth to come from the globalisation of our investment banking and cards businesses and we will also be actively looking for opportunities to expand our funds management operations," he said.

ANZ reported a net profit of A$1.12 billion for the year to September 30, up from A$1.05 billion in the previous year, but said when it released its results in November that it expected margins to contract further in the year ahead.
Meanwhile, the ANZ said it was not looking to take over another bank or be a takeover target itself.
"We are not looking to take over another bank. We are not looking to be taken over," Goode said.
The ANZ would use retained earnings to fund future growth and aimed to keep its dividend payout ratio at about 55 percent to keep growing those retained earnings.
"The main criteria will be our capital needs and we see that as giving the capital, without going to shareholders, to continue to grow this business," Goode said.
"I think it (dividend payout ratio) will stay much the same for this bank, we have growth opportunities ... internationally in particular," he said.

Goode was responding to a question from the Australian shareholders Association, which asked if the bank could increase its payout ratio to match the Commonwealth Bank of Australia's 78 percent ratio.
He also said that the ANZ wanted to keep its capital adequacy ratio at between 6.5 and seven percent to maintain its AA credit rating.
The ANZ's shares were up two cents at A$7.95 at 2.10 p.m. (0310 GMT).
-- Melbourne bureau 61-3 9286-1421
